name: Wondering About Pi
numbering: Issue n of a series is its constant to n decimal places.

e.name: The e Supplement
e.label: Supplement
e.about: Growth, rising, and things that compound.

issues.title: π
issues.clip: Every digit is exact, and there is always another: an infinite courtesy.

uses.hand: Measure across a round pan and multiply by a little over three to know how much ribbon goes around it. A 10-inch pan takes about 31½ inches.
uses.table: Every round thing on the table, plate or glass rim, carries the same ratio. Anyone with a string can check.
uses.work: Some ratios do not depend on size. When something works the same at every scale, find out what it is keeping constant.
uses.mind: There is a digit of π no one has ever looked at, and it is already decided.

issues.clip: Close is not cheap. Close is hospitality.

uses.hand: A 7-inch plate is 22 inches around, near enough. Multiply a width by 22, divide by 7, and you are within a hair.
uses.table: An answer someone can use now is often kinder than an exact one that arrives late.
uses.work: Before chasing precision, say how close is close enough. One part in 2,500 has served for two thousand years.
uses.mind: Archimedes knew his answer was wrong, and exactly how wrong. That is its own kind of knowing.

issues.title: Pie
issues.clip: A pie that waits for the knife is a theorem with a crust.

uses.hand: Moving a 9-inch recipe into a 10-inch tin? The bigger tin holds about a quarter more, so scale the filling up by a quarter.
uses.table: The first slice always comes out untidy. Serve it to the baker.
uses.work: A recipe is a claim anyone with an oven can test. Write methods down so someone else could bake them.
uses.mind: π cannot be finished. A pie has to be. Most good things are one or the other.

issues.clip: No fraction with a smaller denominator comes closer.

uses.hand: Write 113355, split it down the middle, and put the second half over the first. That is π to six places, with no calculator.
uses.table: For roughly nine hundred years after Zu Chongzhi, no one on record had a closer value.
uses.work: A big jump in effort for a small gain means the good version has already been found. After 355/113, the next better fraction needs five-digit numbers.
uses.mind: He reached it by hand, working with polygons of more than twelve thousand sides.

issues.title: Crust
issues.dek: The edge grows more slowly than the middle.
issues.clip: The ratio is not a matter of taste. It is a matter of radius.

uses.hand: One 18-inch pizza holds more than two 12-inch pizzas. Square the widths and compare: 324 against 288.
uses.table: Whoever loves the crust should ask for the small pie.
uses.work: In anything that grows outward, the part touching the outside grows more slowly than the whole. Plan for the middle.
uses.mind: A pie the size of a town would be nearly all filling. A pie the size of a coin would be nearly all crust.

issues.title: Needles
issues.clip: Floors have been answering it ever since.

uses.hand: Any stick and any parallel lines will do, as long as the lines are one stick-length apart. A hundred drops often lands within a quarter of π.
uses.table: Two people dropping toothpicks can race to the better π. Whoever loses has still found π.
uses.work: A steady number can hide inside a pile of random events. Count enough small things and it shows itself.
uses.mind: π is in the kitchen floor, waiting for someone to drop something.

issues.title: Slice
issues.dek: Half the radius, times the crust.
issues.clip: The rule holds for any slice, of any pie, cut by anyone.

uses.hand: For six slices, cut straight through the middle along the hands of a clock at 12, at 2, and at 4.
uses.table: One person cuts and the other chooses first. It is the oldest known way to make a division fair.
uses.work: A rule that holds however the cut is made is a rule you can hand to someone else.
uses.mind: Cut a pie into more and more slices and lay them point to crust, alternating. They become a rectangle: half the edge long and one radius tall. That is where πr² comes from.

issues.title: The Square
issues.dek: The one shape it will not become.
issues.clip: The circle keeps its area. It only declines to be squared.

uses.hand: A 9-inch round pan and an 8-inch square pan hold almost the same, within about half a percent. The kitchen squares the circle close enough.
uses.table: Some questions are answered by proving they cannot be. That is still an answer, and it lets everyone stop.
uses.work: When a goal keeps failing, check whether the tools allow it at all. Change the tools before blaming the effort.
uses.mind: The attempts turned up other discoveries along the way. A problem can be worth having even when it cannot be solved.

issues.title: Patience
issues.dek: One, minus a third, plus a fifth, and so on.
issues.clip: Exact is not the same as quick.

uses.hand: Count along if you like. Ten steps leaves you off by about a tenth; a hundred, by about a hundredth.
uses.table: Everyone at the table can add the next fraction. No one finishes. Everyone gets closer.
uses.work: Here each new correct digit costs ten times the steps of the last. Some improvements are priced like that; know the price before starting.
uses.mind: The series is exact and never arrives. It is possible to be completely right and still on the way.

issues.title: Interest
issues.dek: Growth that never stops to count.
issues.clip: e is what growth comes to when it never stops to count.

uses.hand: Divide 72 by a yearly rate to find how many years it takes to double. At 6 percent, about 12.
uses.table: Paying more often always helps, and past monthly it barely does: 2.613 monthly against 2.718 forever.
uses.work: Small gains taken often add up to a ceiling, not to infinity. Know where the ceiling is.
uses.mind: Somewhere between once a year and every instant, the answer stops being a banker’s and becomes a constant.

issues.title: Rise
issues.dek: Half full, one doubling before the top.
issues.clip: The jar is half full one doubling before it overflows.

uses.hand: Put a rubber band around the jar at the level of a freshly fed starter. The band shows when it has doubled.
uses.table: Anything that doubles on a schedule gets away in its last few doublings. Check early.
uses.work: Compounding looks slow for most of its life and sudden at the end. Measure it by the doubling time, not the size.
uses.mind: Doubling every four hours for a week is forty-two doublings: more than four trillion times the start.

houseStyle: Every sentence is meant. The periodical does not wink.
The mathematics is right. When a figure is approximate, say by how much.
Pie is treated with the same care as π.
No reader is described. Write for someone who will pass it on without a synopsis.
Write like a host, not a lecturer. Every issue leaves uses: something for the hand, the table, the work, and the mind.
A figure is an instrument, not an illustration. It should be worth moving.
openQuestions: What is the smallest true thing about π that still surprises?
Which approximation deserves an issue of its own?
Where do π and e meet outside of an equation?
